LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)  -- Those extra service fees tacked on to concert ticket prices -- long a source of grumbling by ticket buyers -- will disappear for millions of seats sold by the largest U.S. concert promoter this summer. Live Nation is awaiting government approval of a merger with giant Ticketmaster. Live Nation launches "No Service Fee Wednesdays" this week for lawn seats at amphitheaters, removing extra fees from 5 million lawn seats for shows at amphitheaters across the United States. Live Nation insisted that the promotion was about selling more tickets and helping music fans hit by hard times, not improving public relations while it waits for government approval of its merger with Ticketmaster. But the promotion could soothe some bad feelings. "People get a little ticked off when they think they're paying $20 for a ticket and as they progress along the various pages of the electronic transaction, they see more fees added a long the way," said Ray Waddell, who writes about live music tours for Billboard magazine. Live Nation will waive fees on lawn seats for 24 hours, beginning at midnight Tuesday local time and lasting through Wednesday. Lawn seat tickets available this week include concerts by Aerosmith, Blink-182, Coldplay, No Doubt, Nickelback, Depeche Mode, Toby Keith, Brad Paisley and many others, Live Nation said. Other shows coming later in the summer include Crosby Stills & Nash, Crue Fest 2, Def Leppard with Poison and Cheap Trick, Jason Mraz, Kid Rock & Lynyrd Skynyrd, Incubus, New Kids on the Block, Nine Inch Nails and Jane's Addiction, Phish, the Dead, Rascall Flats with Darius Rucker, the Allman Brothers Band, the Fray and the Killers. "They're sacrificing quite a lot of revenue here," Waddell said . He estimated that fees add up to about a third of the average price for lawn seats. The economic recession has not seemed to slow the live concert business, which "considering everything else, is going like gangbusters," he said. "It looks like it could be a really strong year," he said. "People want to go to shows. They want to hear music." Every tour offers some type of promotion, he said, including a lot of $10 lawn seats. "This is a business that's pretty flexible when it needs to be," he said. Live Nation began selling tickets to its own concerts only last year, just months before announcing plans to merge with Ticketmaster, the world's largest ticket-seller. Before that, Live Nation promoted shows but had no infrastructure to sell tickets, and it contracted out to Ticketmaster or others to sell them. The Ticketmaster-Live Nation merger plan has drawn criticism. The Justice Department launched an investigation of the proposed merger in February. Neither Live Nation nor Ticketmaster executives would respond to questions about the merger. However, Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff did talk about it before a U.S. Senate subcommittee earlier this year. The merger "will give us greater flexibility in how we promote, market and sell tickets to events," he said. "It will give us a pathway to alternative pricing and fee structures. And we will be better able to develop new and innovative products and services that enhance the fan experience and make all forms of entertainment more accessible to everyone." CNN's Denise Quan contributed to this report.

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN)** — Millions of concertgoers will be able to avoid the additional charges that have long frustrated ticket buyers when purchasing seats for shows promoted by the nation’s largest concert company this summer.

Live Nation, which is waiting for government authorization to merge with ticketing giant Ticketmaster, is introducing “No Service Fee Wednesdays” this week. The offer eliminates added charges on 5 million amphitheater lawn tickets nationwide.

The company said the initiative is intended to increase ticket sales and provide relief to music fans facing financial difficulties—not to improve its image while regulators consider the Ticketmaster merger. Still, the promotion may help ease some consumer resentment.

Ray Waddell, Billboard magazine’s live-touring writer, said customers often become annoyed after selecting what appears to be a $20 ticket, only to encounter additional charges as they move through the different stages of an online purchase.

For 24 hours—from midnight Tuesday in each local time zone through Wednesday—Live Nation will drop the fees on eligible lawn tickets.

This week’s available concerts include Aerosmith, Blink-182, Coldplay, No Doubt, Nickelback, Depeche Mode, Toby Keith and Brad Paisley, along with many other performers, according to Live Nation.

Shows scheduled for later in the summer include Crosby, Stills & Nash; Crue Fest 2; Def Leppard with Poison and Cheap Trick; Jason Mraz; Kid Rock and Lynyrd Skynyrd; Incubus; New Kids on the Block; Nine Inch Nails and Jane’s Addiction; Phish; the Dead; Rascall Flats with Darius Rucker; the Allman Brothers Band; the Fray; and the Killers.

Waddell said Live Nation is giving up a substantial amount of income through the offer. He estimated that service charges account for roughly one-third of the typical lawn-ticket price.

Despite the recession, the live-concert industry does not appear to have lost momentum and, compared with many other sectors, is performing extremely well, Waddell said. He predicted that the year could be particularly strong because audiences still want to attend concerts and listen to live music.

According to Waddell, nearly every tour uses some form of special offer, including many that sell lawn tickets for $10. He described the concert industry as capable of adapting when circumstances demand it.

Live Nation started handling ticket sales for its own concerts only last year. Just a few months later, it announced its intention to combine with Ticketmaster, the largest ticket seller in the world. Previously, Live Nation promoted concerts but lacked its own ticket-distribution system, so it hired Ticketmaster or other companies to manage sales.

The proposed Live Nation-Ticketmaster combination has faced criticism, and the Justice Department opened an inquiry into the deal in February.

Executives from both companies declined to answer questions about the planned merger. Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff, however, discussed it earlier this year during testimony before a U.S. Senate subcommittee.

Azoff said the combined company would have more freedom in promoting and marketing events and in selling tickets. He also said the deal would make different pricing methods and fee arrangements possible, while helping the companies create innovative services and products that improve fans’ experiences and make entertainment of all kinds available to a broader audience.

CNN’s Denise Quan contributed to the report.

# Live Nation drops service fees on 5 million lawn seats amid Ticketmaster merger review

**NEW YORK —** Live Nation is temporarily eliminating service fees on millions of amphitheater lawn tickets, a promotion unveiled as the concert promoter awaits regulatory approval for its proposed merger with Ticketmaster Entertainment.

The company said its “No Service Fee Wednesdays” program will cover more than 5 million lawn seats at participating Live Nation amphitheaters. Fans who purchase eligible tickets on Wednesdays will pay the advertised ticket price without the service fees that often increase the final cost of attending a concert.

The offer is designed to encourage ticket sales during a period of economic uncertainty, when consumers are cutting back on discretionary spending and the live-music business is competing for tighter entertainment budgets.

Service fees have long been a source of frustration for concertgoers, who can see a ticket’s price rise substantially during the checkout process. Live Nation said the Wednesday promotion is intended to make concerts more affordable and provide customers with clearer pricing.

The initiative comes as federal regulators review Live Nation’s planned merger with Ticketmaster, the dominant ticketing company in the United States. The proposed deal would combine Live Nation’s concert-promotion and venue operations with Ticketmaster’s ticket-distribution business.

The companies have argued that the merger would create a more efficient entertainment company capable of offering artists and fans better services. Critics, including some consumer advocates and music-industry groups, have warned that the combination could reduce competition and give the merged company too much control over concert promotion, venues and ticket sales.

Live Nation’s promotion is separate from the regulatory review, but its timing places additional attention on ticket pricing and fees — two issues central to the public debate over the merger.

The no-fee offer applies only to designated lawn seats purchased on Wednesdays and may not cover other charges, premium seating or tickets sold through resale platforms. Availability also depends on the concert and venue.

Live Nation did not say whether the program would become permanent.

## Live Nation’s “No Service Fee Wednesdays”

In June 2009, amid recession-weakened concert sales, Live Nation launched a promotion waiving its online ticket-service fees on Wednesdays. Tickets had to be purchased through LiveNation.com for selected summer performances at more than 50 participating North American amphitheaters. The offer generally covered both reserved and lawn seats, subject to availability.

The promotion removed Live Nation’s normal convenience charge—which could add several dollars or more to each ticket—but did not necessarily eliminate every possible venue, parking, delivery, charity, or premium-ticket charge. Face-value ticket prices were unchanged.

### Eligible summer tours

The announced roster included selected dates by:

- Aerosmith  
- blink-182  
- Coldplay  
- Crüe Fest 2  
- Dave Matthews Band  
- Def Leppard  
- Depeche Mode  
- Green Day  
- Incubus  
- Jason Mraz  
- Jimmy Buffett  
- Kid Rock and Lynyrd Skynyrd  
- Kings of Leon  
- Nickelback  
- Nine Inch Nails and Jane’s Addiction  
- No Doubt  
- O.A.R.  
- Phish  
- Rascal Flatts  
- REO Speedwagon and Styx  
- The Dead  
- The Fray  
- Toby Keith  

Eligibility varied by venue and performance, and not every date on an artist’s tour was included.

## Industry reaction

Fans generally welcomed the chance to avoid one of the most unpopular parts of concert pricing. Industry observers, however, viewed the move as more than a consumer-friendly gesture:

- **Sales stimulus:** The promotion was designed to move unsold summer inventory during an economic downturn and encourage spending on parking, food, drinks, and merchandise once customers entered Live Nation venues.
- **Competitive positioning:** Live Nation had recently introduced its own ticketing system after ending its principal ticketing arrangement with Ticketmaster. Waiving fees helped draw customers to LiveNation.com and demonstrate that it could compete in primary ticketing.
- **Questions about sustainability:** Analysts noted that service fees were an important source of ticketing revenue, making a permanent, across-the-board elimination unlikely.
- **Merger skepticism:** Independent promoters, consumer advocates, and some lawmakers argued that a temporary fee holiday did not prove prices would decline if Live Nation and Ticketmaster combined. They feared the merged company would have greater power over artists, venues, ticket distribution, and fees.

## The proposed Ticketmaster merger

The promotion came while Live Nation and Ticketmaster were seeking approval for an all-stock merger announced in February 2009. The proposed company, Live Nation Entertainment, would combine:

- Live Nation’s concert promotion and extensive venue network;
- Ticketmaster’s dominant primary-ticketing operation; and
- Ticketmaster’s Front Line artist-management business.

The companies argued that integration would reduce costs, improve ticket distribution, give artists more direct access to fans, and create stronger competition with resale platforms and other entertainment businesses.

Opponents countered that the deal would join two companies that had only recently begun competing against each other. They warned the combined company could bundle promotion, venue access, artist management, and ticketing; disadvantage independent venues and promoters; and face less pressure to reduce service fees.

The merger underwent congressional and Justice Department scrutiny. It was ultimately approved with conditions in January 2010, creating Live Nation Entertainment.

## Live Nation offers $30 fee-free lawn tickets as concert giant works to soften its image

Music fans looking for a less expensive way into outdoor concerts this summer can buy selected Live Nation tickets for $30, with service charges included in the advertised price.

The company’s “Ticket to Summer” promotion covers more than 1,000 concerts at participating venues, including many shows at Live Nation-operated amphitheaters where the discounted inventory is generally located on the lawn. The offer spans rock, country, pop, hip-hop and other genres, although eligible artists and availability vary by market.

Fans can find the tickets through Live Nation’s Ticket to Summer webpage or by searching for participating concerts on LiveNation.com. After selecting a show, buyers should look for ticket types marked as part of the $30 promotion. No promotional code is generally required.

The $30 price is “all-in,” meaning Live Nation’s standard ticketing fees are already included. Taxes may still be added where required, and extras such as parking, premium seating, food, drinks and ticket insurance are not part of the deal.

Inventory is limited and is available while supplies last. For popular concerts, the discounted lawn allotment may disappear quickly even when other, more expensive tickets remain on sale. Fans should also check whether a lawn ticket provides general-admission access and review venue policies on chairs, blankets, bags and weather delays.

### How to buy the discounted tickets

Fans should take the following steps:

1. Visit Live Nation’s Ticket to Summer page or LiveNation.com.
2. Search by city, venue or artist.
3. Select a concert listed as participating in the promotion.
4. Choose the ticket option labeled “$30 Ticket to Summer” or a similar promotional designation.
5. Review the seat location. At amphitheaters, the offer will often be for general-admission lawn access.
6. Confirm the final total before completing the purchase.

Buyers should use Live Nation’s official site or app if they want the promotional price. Tickets displayed on resale marketplaces may be listed at a markup and may carry separate buyer fees.

The offer is also not the same as a season-long lawn pass. A $30 promotional ticket admits the buyer to one selected concert, while venue lawn-pass programs—where available—typically cover multiple shows and have different rules and prices.

### A response to the cost of going to concerts

The promotion arrives as fans continue to complain about the price of live entertainment. Ticket buyers have long criticized “drip pricing,” in which an attractive initial price rises sharply after service, facility and processing charges appear during checkout.

An all-in $30 price is designed to remove that frustration. It gives consumers a clear figure before they begin the purchase process and provides a relatively affordable option at a time when tickets for major tours can cost hundreds of dollars.

For Live Nation, the promotion also has a practical business purpose. Lawn sections at large amphitheaters can hold thousands of people, and filling otherwise unsold space generates additional spending on parking, food, drinks and merchandise. A low-priced lawn ticket can therefore bring in customers who would not have attended at the regular price while creating revenue elsewhere inside the venue.

### Why it could help Live Nation’s public image

The campaign may offer Live Nation a reputational benefit as well.

Live Nation and its Ticketmaster subsidiary have become central targets of consumer anger over ticket prices, service charges, resale markups and access to high-demand events. The scrutiny intensified after high-profile ticket-sale problems and amid broader questions about how much control the company exercises over ticketing, concert promotion and major venues.

The U.S. Justice Department sued Live Nation in 2024, accusing the company of monopolistic practices and seeking structural changes, including a potential separation from Ticketmaster. Live Nation has denied the allegations and has argued that artists, teams and venues—not Ticketmaster alone—set most ticket prices.

Against that backdrop, a widely advertised fee-inclusive ticket allows the company to present itself as addressing one of fans’ most visible complaints. Even if the promotion covers only limited inventory, shoppers who successfully buy a ticket for the stated price may come away with a more favorable view of the company.

The offer also gives Live Nation a chance to emphasize all-in pricing, an approach that consumer advocates have pushed as a way to make ticket shopping more transparent. Advertising the total price upfront is easier to understand than showing a low base price and adding mandatory charges later.

Still, the campaign is unlikely to end criticism by itself. The tickets are limited, many are for distant lawn sections, and the promotion does not address broader concerns about competition, venue contracts, resale markets or the price of premium seats. Fans who miss the discounted allotment may still face substantially higher prices.

For consumers, however, the immediate calculation is simpler: those willing to sit on the lawn, shop early and remain flexible about artists and dates may be able to attend a major summer concert for $30 before applicable taxes—without seeing the price jump because of mandatory ticketing fees at checkout.

A fan who is prepared to spend $50 may abandon the purchase when the total climbs closer to $70 after fees, parking and transportation are included.

The recession’s effect on live music has not been uniform. Major tours by superstar artists can continue to generate strong grosses, supported by affluent buyers and fans who view a concert as a rare event. But strength at the top can obscure softer attendance elsewhere. Developing acts, midlevel performers, clubs and secondary markets are often more exposed when consumers reduce the number of shows they attend.

“People may still go to concerts, but they become more selective about which shows they consider essential,” Waddell said **[VERIFY EXACT QUOTE AND SOURCE]**.

That selectivity creates a difficult equation for promoters. Tours have significant fixed costs, including artist guarantees, transportation, production crews, venue rentals and security. Cutting ticket prices can stimulate demand but may also make it harder to cover those expenses. Holding prices steady, meanwhile, risks leaving more seats empty.

Fees complicate the calculation because they are not always presented as part of the headline price. Promoters and ticketing companies say the charges cover technology, customer service, venue operations and other costs. Critics argue that dividing the price into multiple components makes comparison shopping harder and allows tickets to appear cheaper than they ultimately are.

The most useful measure of the recession’s impact may therefore be attendance rather than gross revenue alone. Higher ticket prices and premium packages can keep overall grosses elevated even as fewer tickets are sold. A tour can look successful in dollar terms while still reaching fewer fans.

Others have experimented with all-in pricing, which displays the full cost earlier in the purchasing process. Such measures may sacrifice some revenue per customer, but they can reduce checkout shock and build goodwill.

Concerts offer an experience that cannot be replicated by a recording or livestream, and fans often continue spending on a small number of personally important events. The challenge is convincing them that the experience is worth not merely the ticket’s advertised price, but the full amount charged.

As Waddell put it, **“[INSERT VERIFIED BILLBOARD QUOTATION ABOUT VALUE, PRICING OR THE RESILIENCE OF CONCERT DEMAND].”**

In a recession, that question of value becomes central. Fans may still want the music, but every added fee gives them another reason to stay home.

## Live Nation waives fees as Ticketmaster deal faces antitrust scrutiny

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — Live Nation is using one of concertgoers’ biggest complaints — ticketing fees — to boost summer sales, offering a limited promotion that removes service charges from selected lawn seats at its U.S. amphitheaters.

The “No Service Fee Wednesday” campaign applied to qualifying tickets purchased on Wednesdays during the promotion. Shows involving major touring acts including **Coldplay, Aerosmith, Nickelback, Kid Rock and Def Leppard** were among those advertised, although availability varied by venue and performance. Taxes, parking charges and other costs could still apply.

The offer came as the recession weighed on discretionary spending and as Live Nation sought to attract fans who had grown frustrated by fees that could add substantially to a ticket’s advertised price.

### Live Nation’s move into ticketing

Live Nation was historically best known as the world’s largest concert promoter and venue operator. For years, it relied on Ticketmaster to sell tickets to many of its events. That relationship changed when Live Nation declined to renew its Ticketmaster agreement and launched its own ticketing platform in 2009.

The move briefly created a significant competitor to Ticketmaster in the primary-ticketing market. But shortly after Live Nation entered the business, the two companies announced plans to combine in an all-stock transaction and form **Live Nation Entertainment**.

The companies argued that merging promotion, venues, artist services and ticketing would reduce costs and make it easier to market concerts. Critics countered that the deal would place too much of the live-entertainment industry under one roof and could weaken competition rather than lower prices.

### Justice Department review

The proposed merger drew an antitrust investigation by the **U.S. Justice Department**, which examined whether combining Ticketmaster’s dominant ticketing operation with Live Nation’s concert-promotion and venue network would harm rivals, artists or consumers.

Regulators focused on the companies’ ability to use control over venues, tours and ticket distribution to pressure performers and competing promoters. State attorneys general, lawmakers and consumer advocates also raised concerns about service fees, ticket availability and Ticketmaster’s influence over both primary and resale markets.

The Justice Department ultimately approved the merger in January 2010 under a consent decree. The settlement required Ticketmaster to license ticketing technology to a rival, divest a ticketing subsidiary and refrain from retaliating against venues that used competing services.

The agreement did not end federal scrutiny. The department later alleged that Live Nation had violated the decree by pressuring venues over their choice of ticketing provider. The decree was subsequently extended and strengthened, and broader antitrust concerns eventually led the Justice Department and a coalition of states to sue Live Nation Entertainment in 2024, seeking structural relief, including a potential breakup of Live Nation and Ticketmaster.
